So you've built your semi-submersible seastead and a big storm has cropped up. So you head below, batten down the hatches and settle into a good book. What's going to be the most important thing over the next few hours? Oxygen, right? Wrong. CO2 poisoning will kill most animals long before they use up the local available oxygen, humans included. We've evolved a number of biological warning signals to alert us to this danger, all of which are extremely uncomfortable and painful, so it's not a problem you want to have to deal with when 30 meter waves are pounding over your head and your snorkel has been snapped off like a matchstick (by contrast, the effects of hyoxia are pretty tame, even enjoyable if you're into that kind of thing). Even when surfaced, CO2 presents dangers to a seastead with a significant portion of it's living space below the surface: CO2 is heavier than air, and can become concentrated in spaces who's ventilation is overhead.

So what can we do? Well, fortunately there are many industrial solutions to capturing CO2 from air, aided in no small part by the recent concern over global warming (well founded or not, it works to our purposes here). These range from lithium hydroxide canisters used in space, to rebreather units used by divers under the ocean's surface. These solutions are, however, somewhat expensive, and not really in line with the DIY ethic of low road seasteading, but never fear, here is a list of home-made alternatives which will keep your air fresh and clean...

Activated carbon

  • Cheap

  • Reusable (you can "regenerate" the carbon by passing low CO2 air over it)

  • Can't find a source, but I've read that it also stores and releases oxygen

Soda lime

  • Cheap

  • Efficient

  • Not resuable

Algae

  • Cheap

  • Reusable

  • Produces oxygen! :)

  • Space inefficient

  • Requires light source

Sugar cane and Ferns

  • Cheap

  • Reusable

  • Self building, no assembly required :p

  • Looks nice

  • Produces oxygen! :)

  • Requires light source

  • Even less space-efficient than algae

I'm Nick, and I'm nineteen years old. When I was nine I had a catastrophic allergic reaction which completely FUCKED my immune system, and it started attacking its own blood cells (specifically the phospholipids, for those interested).

As a result, I got blood clots just about everywhere. After two months in a coma and six months in Intensive Care, I was released from the hospital, but not before the clots had robbed me of the functionality of my left lung and a small portion of my right.

As time went by I got used to it, but the human body wasn't meant to run on only one lung, so after a while, my heart started having trouble keeping up.

When I was sixteen, I was diagnosed with stage 3b heart failure (which, by the way, is a pretty fucking intense diagnosis). It is only because I was fortunate enough to have a friend of a friend make a connection to an incredibly specialized doctor that I am alive today.

Right now, I'm sitting in Children's Hospital of Philadelphia for my quarterly appointment with said specialist, getting anticoagulants pumped into my left arm.

I'm studying to become an American Sign Language translator, but I work as a phlebotomist (one of those guys who puts needles in your arm to take blood).

TL;DR: My immune system killed my lung when I was nine, and it tried to take my heart down with it. It didn't and now I take peoples blood because my own nearly took me (not really, it's just a job).

when the ambassador had finally closed the great wooden doors behind him, the third guest emerged from thin air, unfolding himself from nothing. black clothed, wiry and humming innocously with the right energy, like static electricity. the goblet he held was still a quarter full of red wine so rare. the surprise appointment had been sudden from the ambassador, but the illusion required they did not realize, that this other meeting was happening.
